quests.instruction: Which bones do two jobs at once: they guard your heart and lungs, and they move up and out each time you breathe?
quests.hint: They curve around your chest.
quests.explanation: Ribs form a cage that protects the heart and lungs, and they swing a little as your chest muscles pull, which helps air flow in and out.
quests.funFact: The joints at the back of the ribs let them move a bit like the handle of a bucket.

quests.instruction: Which liquid carries oxygen to every part of you and also carries the cells that fight germs?
quests.hint: It flows in tubes all around your body.
quests.explanation: Blood holds red blood cells that carry oxygen, white blood cells that fight germs, and platelets, all floating in a watery liquid.
quests.funFact: More than half of your blood is a pale yellow liquid called plasma.

quests.instruction: Which part of your body is a shared passage, carrying both the food you swallow and the air you breathe, before they go their separate ways?
quests.hint: Food and air both pass through it before they split up.
quests.explanation: The throat is a shared passage at the back of the mouth. Below it, air goes down the windpipe and food goes down the food pipe.
quests.funFact: An adult's throat is about twelve centimeters long.

quests.instruction: When you shiver, you are making heat with the same parts that move your bones. What are they?
quests.hint: They are what you build when you exercise.
quests.explanation: Muscles pull on bones to move you, and the energy they use gives off heat, which is why shivering warms you up.
quests.funFact: Even when you sit still, small muscle movements make some of your body heat.

quests.instruction: It is a tunnel of small bones that guards the spinal cord, yet it can still bend and twist. What is it?
quests.hint: It is made of many small bones.
quests.explanation: The small bones of the spine form a tunnel for the spinal cord, and the joints and cushions between them let you bend and twist.
quests.funFact: A baby is born with one long curve in the spine, and it gains its other curves as the baby learns to hold up its head and to sit.

quests.instruction: Which parts hold you up, protect your organs, and make new blood cells inside them?
quests.hint: They are hard on the outside and spongy in the middle.
quests.explanation: Bones support the body, shield soft organs, and their marrow makes blood cells.
quests.funFact: Your bones also store calcium and give some back to the blood when it is needed.

quests.instruction: Imagine your diaphragm stopped moving. Which parts would stop getting fresh air pulled in?
quests.hint: They fill with air when the diaphragm moves down.
quests.explanation: The up-and-down movement of the diaphragm pulls air into the lungs, so without it, the lungs could not fill properly.
quests.funFact: The diaphragm is the main muscle of breathing, and it works without you thinking about it.

quests.instruction: Imagine the optic nerve in one eye were cut. Which part would no longer get pictures from that eye?
quests.hint: It turns signals into the pictures you notice.
quests.explanation: The optic nerve carries signals from the eye to the brain, so without it, the brain gets no picture from that eye.
quests.funFact: The other eye can still send pictures, so the person can still see.

quests.instruction: Imagine the epiglottis did not fold down when you swallow. Food could slip into which tube by mistake?
quests.hint: It is the tube that should carry only air.
quests.explanation: The epiglottis covers the windpipe during swallowing. If it did not, food could go down the wrong way and cause choking.
quests.funFact: A baby's voice box sits higher in the throat, which lets a baby breathe and swallow milk at nearly the same time.

quests.instruction: Imagine your pupils stayed tiny in a dim room. Which layer at the back of your eye would get too little light to see well?
quests.hint: It is where the picture lands at the back of the eye.
quests.explanation: Small pupils let in only a little light, so the retina has less to work with and the room looks darker.
quests.funFact: Pupils can open from about two millimeters wide in bright light to about eight in the dark.

quests.instruction: If a cast on a broken arm is too tight, blood flow drops first to which parts, making them cold, pale, or tingly? A grown-up must be told right away.
quests.hint: They are at the very end of the arm.
quests.explanation: A tight cast can squeeze blood vessels, and the parts farthest down the arm feel it first. Always tell a grown-up if fingers change color, feel numb, or hurt.
quests.funFact: A cast should be snug but never tight, and you should be able to wiggle your fingers.

quests.instruction: Imagine the smooth cartilage in your knee wore away completely. Which parts would rub together painfully?
quests.hint: They are the hard parts inside the joint.
quests.explanation: Cartilage cushions the ends of the bones. Without it, bone would rub on bone.
quests.funFact: That is why joints are cushioned and oiled, to help them last a lifetime.

quests.instruction: A ball flies toward you. Your eyes see it, something decides to catch it, and your muscles move. Which part is the one in the middle?
quests.hint: It decides what to do with the message.
quests.explanation: The eyes send the picture, the brain decides, and the muscles carry out the order, in that order.
quests.funFact: All of that can happen in about a fifth of a second.

quests.instruction: Blood leaves the heart through arteries and returns through veins. In between, it passes through which tiny vessels?
quests.hint: They connect the smallest arteries to the smallest veins.
quests.explanation: Capillaries link arteries to veins, and this is where oxygen and nutrients leave the blood to feed the cells.
quests.funFact: A pinched fingertip turns pale and then red again, because blood refills its capillaries when you let go.

quests.instruction: Sound waves shake the eardrum. Next, three tiny linked bones pass the shaking on toward the cochlea. What are those tiny bones called?
quests.hint: They are the smallest bones in your body.
quests.explanation: The ear bones pass the eardrum's vibrations along and make them stronger before they reach the cochlea.
quests.funFact: Their names, hammer, anvil, and stirrup, come from their shapes.

quests.instruction: Several parts team up to keep you balanced. Which of these is not one of them?
quests.hint: It is busy with taste, not balance.
quests.explanation: Your eyes, your inner ear, and sensors in your muscles and joints all send balance messages to the brain. The tongue is for tasting and talking.
quests.funFact: Closing your eyes makes standing on one foot harder, because your brain loses one of its balance clues.

quests.instruction: Arteries, veins, and capillaries all carry blood. Which of these tubes carries air instead?
quests.hint: It branches inside the lungs.
quests.explanation: The bronchi carry air into the lungs. Blood travels in blood vessels.
quests.funFact: An adult takes in about half a liter of air with each ordinary breath.

quests.instruction: Biceps, triceps, and hamstrings are muscles. Which tough cord, one that joins muscle to bone, is not a muscle?
quests.hint: It works like a rope.
quests.explanation: Tendons are tough cords that attach muscles to bones. They are not muscles, but they pass the muscle's pull to the bone.
quests.funFact: The Achilles tendon is named for a hero in Greek myth whose one weak spot was his heel.

quests.instruction: I am red, I carry oxygen, and I am made in bone marrow. What am I?
quests.hint: I am shaped like a tiny disk.
quests.explanation: Red blood cells are made in bone marrow and carry oxygen from the lungs to every part of the body.
quests.funFact: Red blood cells have no nucleus, which leaves more room for carrying oxygen.

quests.instruction: I am tiny, I am made in bone marrow, and I clump together to plug a cut. What am I?
quests.hint: I am not a whole cell but a small piece of one.
quests.explanation: Platelets are small pieces of cells made in bone marrow. They stick together to seal a cut.
quests.funFact: A single drop of blood holds millions of platelets.

quests.instruction: We are strong bands that join bone to bone and keep joints from slipping out of place. What are we?
quests.hint: We are not the cords that join muscle to bone.
quests.explanation: Ligaments hold the bones of a joint steady, a bit like straps.
quests.funFact: Stretching a ligament too far is called a sprain.

quests.instruction: Which kind of muscle do you control on purpose, like the muscles that move your arms and legs?
quests.hint: It is attached to bones.
quests.explanation: Skeletal muscles move your bones and obey your choices. You decide when to use them.
quests.funFact: Skeletal muscle is the most common kind of muscle in your body.

quests.instruction: Which kind of muscle lines your stomach and blood vessels and works on its own, without you deciding?
quests.hint: It squeezes slowly and steadily.
quests.explanation: Smooth muscle in the stomach, intestines, and blood vessels squeezes without your control.
quests.funFact: It is called smooth because, under a microscope, it lacks the stripes seen in other muscles.

quests.instruction: Which kind of muscle is found only in the heart?
quests.hint: It never takes a break.
quests.explanation: Cardiac muscle works automatically and squeezes the heart about once every second at rest.
quests.funFact: Heart muscle cells can keep beating on their own, even in a dish in a laboratory.

quests.instruction: Which butterfly-shaped gland at the front of your neck helps control how fast your body uses energy?
quests.hint: It sits just below the voice box.
quests.explanation: The thyroid makes hormones that set the pace of your body's energy use.
quests.funFact: Iodine, found in iodized salt and seafood, helps the thyroid make its hormones.

quests.instruction: Which pea-sized gland under the brain is called the master gland, because its hormones tell other glands what to do?
quests.hint: It hangs from the base of the brain.
quests.explanation: The pituitary sends out hormones that control growth and tell other glands, such as the thyroid, when to work.
quests.funFact: Its hormones help control how tall you grow.

quests.instruction: Which tiny gland deep in the brain makes melatonin, the hormone that helps you feel sleepy at night?
quests.hint: It responds to darkness.
quests.explanation: The pineal gland makes more melatonin when it is dark, which helps your body know that it is time to sleep.
quests.funFact: Bright light at night, including light from screens, can lower melatonin.

quests.instruction: Which small glands sit on top of your kidneys like little hats and make adrenaline?
quests.hint: Their name means near the kidney.
quests.explanation: The adrenal glands release adrenaline when you are excited or scared.
quests.funFact: You have two of them, one on top of each kidney.

quests.instruction: Which organ belongs to two systems at once, because it makes digestive juices and also makes the hormone insulin?
quests.hint: It has one foot in the digestive system and one in the hormone system.
quests.explanation: The pancreas helps digest food and also helps control blood sugar with insulin.
quests.funFact: Only a small part of the pancreas makes hormones, and the rest makes digestive juices.

quests.instruction: Pee is made in the kidneys and stored in the bladder. Which two thin tubes carry it from one to the other?
quests.hint: There is one for each kidney.
quests.explanation: The ureters are two thin tubes that carry pee from the kidneys down to the bladder, squeezing it along in little waves.
quests.funFact: Each ureter is about as long as a ruler.
